findings.problem: TODO declares 'use Rayon and SmallVec because it will be faster' without any workload specification, baseline measurement, or benchmark evidence. This directly violates the Holzman Rust performance discipline: 'Do not cargo-cult Rayon, SmallVec, Cow, zero-copy, manual loops, or iterator chains. Use them because the workload, lifetime, allocation budget, or benchmark supports them.'
findings.failure_mode: Introducing Rayon for a 4-element fixed-size input will add thread-pool scheduling overhead, mutex contention, and task creation costs that dwarf any per-element savings, producing measurable slowdown. Adding SmallVec without measured hot-path data is speculative optimization that adds a dependency and compile-time cost with no proven benefit.
findings.fix: Remove the TODO. If a performance improvement is needed, first define the workload (input distribution, throughput target, latency SLA), measure the current baseline with a benchmark, use a profiler to identify the actual hot path, and only then justify Rayon/SmallVec with evidence showing the benefit exceeds their overhead.

findings.problem: Function returns Vec<&'static str> for a fixed 4-byte input. This always allocates on the heap (minimum capacity 1 element, but typically more due to Vec growth strategy), even when all data fits on the stack.
findings.failure_mode: Every call to classify_four performs at least one heap allocation (Vec::new + allocator call). For a fixed-size 4-element input, this is unnecessary allocation overhead. If SmallVec were introduced per the TODO, it would need to be justified by measured hot-path distribution showing the small-size case is dominant.
findings.fix: Either keep the return type as Vec and accept the allocation (documented trade-off), or if SmallVec is introduced, require a benchmark proving the small-size case dominates and the stack-based path reduces measurable latency. The current function signature and implementation are functionally correct; the question is whether the allocation cost matters for this workload.
